title: Teaching Number Recognition to Grade 1 (1 to 20, the Right Way) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Number Recognition Grade 1: Teach 1 to 20 + Quiz
meta_desc: A parent-friendly guide to number recognition for Grade 1: read and write numerals 1 to 20, fix reversed digits, plus a free 8-question quiz to try.
excerpt: A child can chant one-two-three all day and still not know which shape on the page is a 7. Number recognition is a separate skill — here is how to teach reading and writing numerals 1 to 20, with a quick quiz to check.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Here is a scene I have watched play out at hundreds of kitchen tables. A four- or five-year-old rattles off ‘one, two, three, four, five’ without a pause, and the parent beams. Then you point at the numeral 4 sitting alone on a flashcard and ask ‘which number is this?’ — and the child goes quiet. That gap is the whole point of this article. Number recognition in Grade 1 is not about counting out loud. It is about looking at a printed symbol and instantly knowing that this squiggle is a 7 and that one is a 2, and being able to write them back. Reciting the count-song and reading a numeral are two different skills, and plenty of bright six-year-olds have one without the other.

The good news: number recognition for Grade 1 is one of the most teachable things in early maths, because it responds so well to short, playful, everyday practice. You are teaching the numerals 1 to 20 first — that is the NCERT Grade 1 expectation — and only later stretching to 100. No app required. A pencil, some sand or salt on a tray, and ten minutes will do more than any screen.

Rote counting is not number recognition

The single most common mistake I see is treating the counting rhyme as proof a child knows their numbers. It is not. A child can sing to twenty like a nursery chant and still fail to match the numeral 13 to a pile of thirteen buttons. Real number recognition sits on three legs, and a child needs all three:

  • Reading the numeral — sees 8 on the page and says ‘eight’ without counting up to it.
  • Matching numeral to quantity — knows that 8 means a group of eight things, not just a shape.
  • Writing the numeral — forms the digit correctly, the right way round, starting from the right point.

If your child can do the first but not the second, they have memorised shapes without meaning. If they can count objects but freeze at the printed numeral, they have meaning without the symbol. Both are half a skill.

Match the numeral to the quantity (subitising)

The bridge between a symbol and its meaning is what teachers call subitising — seeing a small group and knowing ‘how many’ at a glance, without counting one-by-one. A child who can look at a dice face and say ‘five’ instantly is subitising. This is the skill that turns 6 from a curly shape into an idea of six-ness.

Build it with dice, dominoes, and ten-frames. Flash five fingers and ask how many before they can count. Lay three coins down, cover them, ask how many were there. Then, and this is the key step, put the numeral card next to the group so the symbol and the quantity live side by side. In my experience teaching six-year-olds, children who do plenty of numeral-to-quantity matching stop reversing digits far sooner, because the digit finally means something to them.

The numerals children reverse and confuse

Some digits are simply harder to write than others, and reversals are completely normal well into Grade 1. They are not a sign of dyslexia and usually fade on their own by age seven or so. But you can speed things up by knowing which ones to watch. The classic troublemakers are 3, 5, 7 and 9, plus the mirror-flip between 6 and 9.

NumeralCommon errorFix that works
3Written backwards, like a capital E curve‘Round the tree, round again’ — both bumps face the same way
5Top line drawn first, whole digit flippedDown the back, round the belly, then the hat last
6 and 9One written as the other (mirror flip)6 has its ball at the bottom; 9 has its ball at the top
7Reversed, or an extra cross-bar addedAcross the top, then slant down — one straight cut
9Loop and tail drawn as a mirror imageCircle first on the left, straight tail down the right

One honest caveat: do not turn a reversed 3 into a crisis. If you frown every time, the child tenses up and it gets worse. Point it out calmly, model the correct stroke once, and move on. Consistency beats correction.

Multisensory tricks that actually stick

Numerals are motor memory as much as visual memory — the hand learns the shape. That is why writing them in different textures beats copying rows of the same digit on lined paper. A few that families I know swear by:

  • Sand or salt tray — spread a thin layer of salt or rava on a steel plate and let the child draw the numeral with a finger. Wrong? Just shake the tray flat and try again. No eraser, no shame.
  • Number hunts — ‘find me all the 4s’ on a page from the newspaper, a calendar, or the TV remote. Recognising numerals in the wild, out of order, is harder and more useful than reading a tidy 1-to-20 chart.
  • Sky writing — trace the digit big in the air with a whole arm, saying the stroke rhyme out loud. The large movement locks in direction.
  • Dotted tracing — trace over dotted numerals with a finger first, pencil second. This is where a good worksheet earns its keep.

Out of order is the real test

Here is a small, counter-intuitive tip that separates children who truly recognise numbers from those who are still leaning on the count-song: always practise numerals out of sequence. A child who can only name 7 by whispering ‘one, two, three…’ up to it has not recognised it — they have re-counted to it. Flashing 14, then 6, then 19 in random order forces genuine recognition, and it exposes exactly which numerals are shaky.

A realistic ten-minute daily routine

You do not need a lesson plan. Two minutes of subitising with dice, three minutes writing two or three tricky numerals in the salt tray, three minutes of a number hunt around the room, and two minutes matching numeral cards to groups of objects. Rotate which numerals you focus on so 3, 5, 7 and 9 get extra turns. Ten minutes a day for a few weeks will move a child from ‘knows the count-song’ to ‘reads and writes 1 to 20’ more reliably than any weekend marathon.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz built around exactly this skill — matching numerals to number-words, spotting which numeral shows a given quantity, choosing the correctly written digit, and simple before-and-after questions. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: Grade 1 Number Recognition Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on reading and writing numerals 1 to 20. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: The word seven is written as the numeral 7.

questions.q: How do you write the number ‘twelve’?
questions.explanation: Twelve is a 1 followed by a 2, written 12. The 21 shape is twenty-one.

questions.q: You see a group of ● ● ● ● dots. Which numeral shows how many?
questions.explanation: There are four dots, so the numeral is 4.

questions.q: Which numeral shows a group of nine objects?
questions.explanation: Nine objects are shown by the numeral 9, which has its ball at the top and a tail going down.

questions.q: Which of these is the numeral 3 written the correct way round?
options: A 3 with both bumps facing left
A 3 with both bumps facing right
questions.explanation: A correct 3 has both curved bumps opening to the left, so the digit itself faces right.
Counting on by one from 15 gives 16, the numeral that comes just after.

questions.q: A 6 and a 9 look alike but flipped. Which sentence is true?
options: 6 has its ball at the top
9 has its ball at the bottom
6 has its ball at the bottom
questions.explanation: The 6 has its round ball at the bottom, while the 9 has its ball at the top. That is how you tell the flip apart.

faq.q: What is the difference between counting and number recognition?
faq.a: Counting is saying the number-words in order, like a song. Number recognition is looking at a printed numeral and knowing what it is, and matching it to a quantity. A child can count to twenty and still not recognise the numeral 13 on the page — the two are separate skills.

faq.q: Why does my Grade 1 child keep writing numbers backwards?
faq.a: Reversals of 3, 5, 7, 9 and the 6 or 9 flip are completely normal until about age seven. It is not usually a sign of a learning problem. Model the correct stroke calmly, practise in a salt tray so mistakes wipe away, and it fades with time.

faq.q: How many numbers should a Grade 1 student recognise?
faq.a: The Grade 1 expectation is confident reading and writing of numerals 1 to 20, then extending towards 100 through the year. Get 1 to 20 solid first — both reading the symbol and writing it — before pushing higher.

faq.q: What is subitising and why does it matter?
faq.a: Subitising is seeing a small group and knowing how many at a glance, without counting one-by-one — like reading a dice face. It matters because it links the numeral to real quantity, which stops children treating digits as meaningless shapes.
